source.title: FedWon: Triumphing Multi-domain Federated Learning Without Normalization

record.file_problem: Full paper text and appendices are present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests normalization-free federated training in a new setting, including CIFAR-10 with skewed labels, but reports test accuracy rather than the training classification error in the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test accuracy and feature-map similarity, not training classification error or convergence to zero training error. The CIFAR-10 results concern federated learning with label skew, not random initialization benchmarks in the versions. The listed versions do not directly describe this tested behavior.
record.test_reason: FedWon applies normalization-free training with scaled weight standardization to federated learning and evaluates its own performance. The accuracy-over-rounds comparisons also change convolution parameterization and sometimes learning rates and gradient clipping; they do not isolate the effect of adding BN or evaluate Fixup. No results test V1–V5.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate but understates the central conclusion: the authors present FedWon primarily as a method for multi-domain federated learning, reporting superior average test accuracy, applicability to cross-silo and cross-device settings, and effective training with very small batches. Label-skew experiments are an additional application.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates federated training with local data partitions, client selection, server aggregation, normalization removal, and scaled weight standardization. Its CIFAR-10 setting uses MobileNetV2 and label skew, rather than the claim versions' centralized training-error tests.
record.method_sensitivity: Label skew changes reported test accuracy; FedWon reports 75.7 in the i.i.d. case and 41.9 under Dir(0.1).

fits_no_version.finding: FedWon reports CIFAR-10 test accuracies of 75.7, 72.8, 70.7 and 41.9 across increasing label skew, compared with FedAvg's 75.0, 64.5, 61.1 and 36.0; cross-silo FedWon accuracy is 76.45%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Removing BN and using scaled weight standardization can improve federated test accuracy under label skew.

fits_no_version.finding: Figure 4 and Appendix Figure 10a are described as showing faster accuracy gains for FedWon than FedAvg and FedBN, respectively, on Digits-Five. These compare complete training recipes.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: FedWon's normalization-free recipe can reach useful test accuracy faster than BN-based federated methods in the evaluated settings.

record.code_released: The source code will be released.
record.problems: The relevant CIFAR-10 outcomes are test accuracies, not training error. Main text Figure 6 does not state uncertainty for its numeric table values; the cross-silo result in Table 15 also reports no uncertainty. The evidence is federated and label-skewed, so it does not test the claim's random-initialization training-error behavior.
record.rows_left_out: Only the reported CIFAR-10 skewed-label results were kept. Other datasets and domains concern multi-domain FL rather than the CIFAR-10 label-distribution experiment, and feature-map similarities and test-accuracy plots do not measure a claim version's stated training-error outcome.

untested.parts: Training classification error, zero-error fitting, corrupted or random labels, and model-size, stopping and regularization effects.
Teacher-student ReLU local minima and the effect of extra student neurons.
Depth-related training degradation, identity-shortcut controls, deep plain tanh initialization and Fixup.
Initialization comparisons measuring signal propagation, learning speed or trainable depth. WSConv is an ongoing weight reparameterization, not an initialization-only comparison.
Initial stability thresholds, loss catapults, curvature trajectories, edge-of-stability dynamics and divergence.
The effect of adding BN to otherwise matched networks on accuracy gain and learning-rate tolerance, and training speed or stability with Fixup.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's T3/tests classification conflicts with its own version assessments. Test accuracy is relevant to V6's speed component, so its exclusion rests on the bundled method comparison, not merely on being a test metric. The omitted accuracy trajectories are already declared in rows_left_out; no missing claim-bearing results require new rows.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not measure training classification error, random-label fitting, or the size, stopping, and regularization conditions in V1.
No two-layer ReLU teacher-student local-minimum experiment or width sweep.
No comparison of plain and residual networks for training error or depth-related degradation.
No comparison of initialization schemes for signal propagation, training speed, or trainable depth.
No learning-rate stability threshold or sharpness analysis.
The paper compares normalization methods in federated learning, but does not test the specified batch-normalization speed or learning-rate-tolerance claim.
